### scRNAseq analysis of mouse IALVs

For scRNAseq analyses of isolated IALVs we used a total of 10 Rosa26mTmG mice, without Cre expression and without tamoxifen treatment, with equivalent representation of sex (five males and five females with ages between 10 and 12 months). Full-length IALVs from both the left and right sides of each Rosa26mTmG mouse were isolated and cleaned of excessive matrix and adipose tissue. Isolated vessels were digested into single-cell suspensions as described above, and the cells were kept on ice following single-cell suspension until all the tissues had been processed. Cells from all vessels were combined and sorted for tdTomato expression to remove debris and concentrate the cells for downstream single-cell 3′ RNA-Seq libraries creation with 10x Genomics Chromium Chip and Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ RNA-Seq reagents. Samples were sequenced with the NovaSeq 6000 S4-PE100 flow cell.

Mus musculus genome GRCm39 and annotation GTF (v106) from Ensembl (https://useast.ensembl.org/Mus_musculus/Info/Index) were used to build the reference index and the reads were processed using Cell Ranger (v7.0.1; Zheng et al., 2017) with default parameters. The quality control and filtering steps were performed using R (v4.2.1; https://www.r-project.org/) as outlined in the Seurat pre-processing steps (Hao et al., 2021; Hao et al., 2024). Ambient RNA was removed from the Cell Ranger output with SoupX (Young and Behjati, 2020). Doublet score for each cell was estimated using scDBlFinder (v1.12.0; Germain et al., 2021). Non-expressed genes (sum zero across all samples) and low-quality cells (>10% mitochondrial genes, <500 genes, <1000 UMIs per cell and doublet score <0.5) were excluded from analysis. Of 10,188 cells, 7435 passed our inclusion criteria and included three dominant clusters including LECs (2962 cells), LMCs (978 cells), and fibroblasts (2261 cells) with the remaining cells comprising immune cells (1147 cells) and some mammary epithelial cell contamination (87 cells). Cells passing filtering were normalized/scaled (SCTransformation), dimensionally reduced (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) and UMAP clustered, and hierarchically analyzed with Seurat (Hao et al., 2021; Hao et al., 2024) with default parameters. To select the optimal cluster resolution, we used Clustree with various resolutions. We examined the resulting tree to identify a resolution where the clusters were well separated and biologically meaningful, ensuring minimal merging or splitting at higher resolutions. Our goal was to find a resolution that captured relevant cell subpopulations while maintaining distinct clusters without excessive fragmentation. Initial clustering of the entire population of cells was done at a resolution of 0.8 and 18 PCs to achieve the UMAP of 0–19 cell clusters as shown in Figure 5a. We used a resolution of 0.5 for sub-clustering LMCs (original groups 5 and 6), 0.87 for LECs (original groups 0, 1, 2, and 11), and 1.0 for fibroblasts (3, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 13). Marker gene expression profile on cell clusters and gene co-expression was visualized using Seurat and ShinyCell R application (Ouyang et al., 2021). The full scRNAseq raw dataset has been uploaded to the NIH GEO under the accession number GSE277843. Differential gene expression within subclusters of LECs, LMCs, and AdvCs was performed using Seurat’s ‘Find Markers’ function and with a minimum of either 40% or 50% cell expression and average log fold change (Log2FC) minimum of 0.5 or 1. When assessing the LMC IP3 receptor genes Itpr1-3 and Itprid2, a percent cell expression of 40% and Log2FC of 0.25 was used. In the volcano plot for LEC subcluster 8 differential gene expression, listed genes had a cutoff of a Log2FC of 2 or –2 to be displayed on the plot.

### Ex vivo Ca2+ imaging with the genetically encoded GCaMP6f indicator

CkitCreERT2, Myh11CreERT2, and PdgfrαCreERTM mice were crossed with GCaMP6f mice in a similar manner as described for Rosa26mTmG. CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f, PdgfrαCreERTM-GCaMP6f, and Myh11CreERT2-GCaMP6f were induced with tamoxifen (10 mg/ml) for 5 consecutive days by i.p. injection. IALVs isolated from CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f, PdgfrαCreERTM-GCaMP6f, and Myh11CreERT2-GCaMP6f were cannulated as described above. The cannulated vessel, with micropipette holders, observation chamber, and V-track mounting system, was transferred to the stage of the spinning disk confocal with a Prime95B scMOS camera (Photometrics), a Cascade II EMCCD (Photometrics), or an Ixon888 EMCCD camera (Andor) for Ca2+ imaging (Castorena-Gonzalez et al., 2018b). Pressures for the input and output cannula were connected to a T-junction which was set briefly to 8 cmH2O and the vessel lengthened to remove axial slack. A peristaltic pump maintained constant perfusion of the observation chamber with Krebs buffer at a rate of 0.5 ml/min while the vessel equilibrated at 37°C for 30–60 min with pressures set to 3 cmH2O. Spontaneous contractions were allowed to stabilize over a period of 30 min to verify normal function and then were blunted with 2 μM wortmannin to limit movement associated with contractions during Ca2+ imaging. A Windows-based computer was used to digitize the pressure transducer signals and video image of the vessel from a firewire camera at 30–40 Hz (Davis et al., 2012). Real-time inner diameter tracking was made with LabVIEW (National Instruments; Austin, TX) (Davis, 2005). Once contractions were <5 µm in amplitude, Ca2+ recordings were made at 20 FPS for 20–40 s.

### Ca2+ imaging and analysis in IALVs over the contraction cycle

Background noise was determined by using the histogram feature of FIJI in a rectangle in a region of the field of view without sample. This value was subtracted from the entire field of view. In some cases, the vessel movement due to contraction was offset with video stabilization with the FIJI plugin Image Stabilizer. A max projection was used to create non-overlapping ROIs of GCaMP6f+ cells for each inducible Cre-GCaMP6f IALV. From these cell ROIs, the ‘reslice z’ function was used to create pseudo-linescan STMs, which were divided by their baseline values to obtain F/F0 values for each individual cell. At least three cells, except in the case of 1 CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f IALV, in which only two cells were observed, were analyzed in this manner for each vessel segment. Max projections of the image stack were then used to create non-overlapping cell masks of 3–5 muscle cells per field of view of one vessel. Ca2+ traces for those cells contained 5–10 contraction cycles and Ca2+ transients and were characterized for peak intensity (expressed as a baseline-referenced ratio, F/F0), frequency, and duration in seconds.

### Analysis of subcellular Ca2+ transients in Myh11CreERT2-GCaMP6f IALVs

For Myh11CreERT2, we performed Ca2+ imaging as above in the presence of 1 µM nifedipine to stop the ‘Ca2+ flashes’ associated with APs (Zawieja et al., 2018a) and focus on the subcellular activity at three different experimental pressures of 0.5, 2, and 5 cmH2O. For this protocol, we used a particle analysis approach to analyze all Ca2+ transients in the field of view. Ca2+ transients in intact vessels were quantified by particle analysis using Volumetry software (version G8d) as previously described (Drumm et al., 2017; Drumm et al., 2019a). Movies of Ca2+ transients in intact vessels were imported into Volumetry software (version G8d) and background subtracted. Movies were smoothed using a Gaussian filter: 1.5 × 1.5 mM, StdDev 1.0. Raw Ca2+ transients were converted to Ca2+ particles (PTCLs) using a flood-fill algorithm as previously described (Drumm et al., 2017; Drumm et al., 2019a). PTCLs <10 µM2 were rejected to facilitate the removal of noise, and then the total PTCL area and PTCL count could be tabulated for each recording.

### Membrane potential recordings in IALVs

Mouse IALVs were isolated and cleaned as described above. IALVs were pressurized in our isobaric myography apparatus and allowed to equilibrate to ensure typical contractile activity was evident. A bolus of wortmannin at 2 µM was then applied to the bath to blunt contraction amplitude below 5 µm. Intracellular recordings of lymphatic muscle were made with microelectrodes (250–300 MΩ) filled with 1 M KCl and an SEC-05x amplifier (NPI) connected to a Grass S48 stimulator, viewed with a Tektronix TDS3052 digital oscilloscope. Membrane potential and diameter were simultaneously recorded using LabVIEW. Membrane potential and APS were allowed to stabilize and then pressure was slowly raised from 0.5 to 2 cmH2O and then 5 cmH2O. In some cases, the electrode dislodged due to the intrinsic contractions of the vessel or wall displacement as pressure was modulated. In these situations, we attempted to re-impale the cell or one of the neighboring cells. Only vessels in which a recording with a minimum of three stable APs was successfully recorded at two of the three experimental pressures were used for subsequent analysis.

We also confirmed LMC impalement using microelectrode filled with 1 M KCl and (100 µg/ml) Biocytin-AF488 (A12924, Thermo Fisher) to label impaled cells that displayed APs, over a 10-min recording period. Following the impalement and loading with Biocytin-AF488, the vessel was transferred to our imaging apparatus for confocal imaging and 3D reconstruction using the Andor Dragonfly 200 and IMARIS. Image stacks were taken with a 25x water objective at 0.5 micron intervals throughout the diameter of the vessel.

### Light activation of ChR2 to stimulate popliteal cLV contractions

As the IALV has a nearly continuous contractile cycle, we utilized the popliteal vessel for its much slower contraction frequency in the experiments testing our ability to trigger a propagated contraction upon stimulation of the enforced expression of ChR2. Popliteal vessels were isolated from CkitCreERT2-ChR2/tdTomato, PdgfrαCreERTM -ChR2/tdTomato, or Myh11CreERT2-ChR2/tdTomato mice (3–9 months of age) as previously described (Scallan and Davis, 2013), although we intentionally retained some connective tissue and adipose tissue to ensure we had a sufficient population of recombined cells to test in the adventitia layer of the vessel. Contractions were allowed to stabilize over a 30-min equilibration period with pressure set to 3 cmH2O. If basal contraction frequency was too high, we applied pinacidil to the bath in 100 nM increments, without exceeding 600 nM, to further slow contraction frequency to around 6 contractions per minute. Pinacidil at sub 1 µM doses can slow contraction frequency without causing overt hyperpolarization of membrane potential (Davis et al., 2020). Supplemental 100 nM doses of pinacidil were applied throughout the experiment to maintain a spontaneous contraction frequency below 6 per minute to allow ample diastolic time for ChR2 stimulation. Throughout this protocol, the popliteal was allowed to contract spontaneously to ensure we had not overly inhibited APs by the pacemaking cells with pinacidil. Occasionally, spontaneous contractions occurred just prior to light-evoked contractions, resulting in a potential false positive, so we performed multiple stimulations over a period of 5–10 min, typically waiting at least 3 s after any spontaneous contraction before stimulating. Care was made to align the light fiber in such a way that only part of the vessel would be directly illuminated and so target cells of interest would be directly activated by 473 nm light using a Laser diode (Doric LD Fiber Light Source, Quebec, Canada), through an optical probe with a 10-µm tip (Doric, OPT_200_0.22.010). To further limit the excitation field, the optical probe was coated with black acrylic paint using an eyelash brush so that the uncoated opening was ~2–3 µm. With the probe positioned within 5 µm of one side of the vessel wall, the spread of light covered an area ~10–100 µm wide on the back side of the vessel (depending on the diode amplitude setting). Light pulses, 200 ms in length, were triggered by a Grass S9 stimulator (Harvard Apparatus, Holliston, MA) connected to the external TTL input of the laser diode. Pulse amplitude was adjusted between 40 and 90 mA using the Laser Diode Module Driver (Doric). A contraction was considered to be triggered if it occurred within 50ms of stimulation. We performed photo-stimulation from 2 to 4 sites within each vessel, with 6–14 stimulations per site. If a photo-stimulation was triggered incidentally after the initiation of a ‘spontaneous contraction’, it was discarded from the analysis. For Myh11CreERT2-ChR2-tdTomato, six vessels from three separate mice were tested. For PdgfrαCreERTM-ChR2-tdTomato, six vessels from four separate mice were tested with a max of two vessels per mouse. For CkitCreERT2-ChR2-tdTomato, seven vessels from three separate mice were assessed. Diameter was recorded to align photo-activation with the contraction cycle using LabVIEW.

### Solutions and chemicals

Krebs buffer was composed of (in mM): 146.9 NaCl, 4.7 KCl, 2 CaCl2, 1.2 MgSO4, 1.2 NaH2PO4·H2O, 3 NaHCO3, 1.5 NaHEPES, and 5 d-glucose (pH = 7.4 at 37°C). Krebs-BSA buffer was prepared with the addition of 0.5% (wt/vol) BSA while Krebs Ca2+-free replaced CaCl2 with 3 mM EGTA. Tamoxifen was dissolved to 10 mg/ml in a Safflower Oil-Ethanol (95–5% vol/vol) solution with rocking agitation, separated into aliquots, and stored at –20°C. Wortmannin was dissolved in DMSO to a stock solution of 1 mM. Pinacidil was dissolved in DMSO to a stock concentration of 1 µM. Nifedipine was dissolved in DMSO to a stock concentration of 1 mM. All chemicals were obtained from Sigma (St. Louis, MO), except for BSA (US Biochemicals; Cleveland, OH), MgSO4, and NaHEPES (Fisher Scientific; Pittsburgh, PA).

### Statistical tests

Statistical differences in the isobaric contractile tests for popliteal cLVs isolated from PdgfrαCreERTM-Ano1fl/fl, PdgfrαCreERTM-Gjc1fl/fl, and PdgfrαCreERTM-Cacna1cfl/fl mice over the various contractile parameters were assessed via (1) repeated measures two-way ANOVAs with Sidak’s multiple comparison tests performed using Prism9 (Graphpad). Data are plotted as mean ± SEM and significance determined at p < 0.05 and 0.10> p > 0.05 were reported. Cre negative mice were used for controls, and experiment order was not randomized aside from random mouse selection from cages housing both Cre+ or Cre− mice. Experimental sample size was determined by the results from our previous experiments assessing Gjc1, Ano1, Cacna1c with Myh11CreERT2 mice. Data from cLVs in which a negative tone value was recorded at any pressure, which typically indicated incomplete relaxation or occluding bubbles in the cannula, were not included in the tone analysis. Vessels that failed to contract at a given pressure had no value recorded for ejection fraction or normalized amplitude, and REML mixed effects model was used in place of repeated measures two-way ANOVA. We used a categorical Chi-squared statistical test for the experiments assessing our ability to trigger a contraction with activation of ChR2+ cells. Ca2+ particle area and frequency were compared using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test. Significance was determined at p < 0.05. A mixed effects analysis with Tukey’s multiple comparison post hoc test was used to compare AP parameters across pressure using Prism9 (GraphPad).

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90679.4.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90679.4.sa2)

Summary:

This is a well written manuscript describing studies directed at identifying the cell type responsible for pacemaking in murine collecting lymphatics. Using state of the art approaches, the authors identified a number of different cell types in the wall of these lymphatics and then using targeted expression of Channel Rhodopsin and GCaMP, the authors convincingly demonstrate that only activation of lymphatic muscle cells produces coordinated lymphatic contraction and that only lymphatic muscle cells display pressure-dependent Ca2+ transients as would be expected of a pacemaker in these lymphatics.

Strengths:

The use of targeted expression of channel rhodopsin and GCaMP to test the hypothesis that lymphatic muscle cells serve as the pacemakers in musing lymphatic collecting vessels.

Weaknesses:

The only significant weakness was the lack of quantitative analysis of most of the imaging data shown in Figures 1-11. In particular the colonization analysis should be extended to show cells not expected to demonstrate colocalization as a negative control for the colocalization analysis that the authors present. These weaknesses have been resolved by revision and addition of new and novel RNAseq data, additional colocalization data and membrane potential measurements.

Comments on revisions: No additional concerns.

results.result: LMCs consistently displayed spontaneous Ca2+ events during diastole that were modulated in a pressure-dependent manner. Ca2+ imaging with Myh11CreERT2-GCaMP6f showed that 100% of LMCs exhibited global Ca2+ flashes, and 20 of 43 LMCs displayed at least one diastolic Ca2+ transient. The frequency and spatial spread of these transients increased with pressure (0.5 to 5 cmH2O), with PTCL area increasing from 73.2±17.7 to 139.2±26.9 µm²/frame and PTCL count increasing from 2.9±0.4 to 5.2±0.6 per frame.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C79-C84 provide converging evidence from Ca2+ imaging experiments showing pressure-dependent diastolic Ca2+ transients specifically in LMCs. The quantitative data on PTCL area and frequency (C83, C84) with statistical significance (p<0.05) support the pressure-dependent modulation. The specificity to LMCs is demonstrated by comparison with other cell types (C81).

results.result: Optogenetic depolarization with ChR2 induced propagated contractions only in LMCs. Photo-stimulation of Myh11CreERT2-ChR2-tdTomato cells triggered contractions in 88.5% of stimulation events, while CkitCreERT2-ChR2-tdTomato (3.25%) and PdgfrαCreERTM-ChR2-tdTomato (3.03%) cells failed to initiate coordinated contractions.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C69-C74 provide strong experimental evidence from optogenetic stimulation experiments. The stark contrast in success rates (88.5% vs ~3%) between LMC stimulation and other cell types, with appropriate controls (non-induced mice at 7%), demonstrates that only LMCs can initiate propagated contractions. The quantitative data and statistical analysis support this conclusion.

results.result: The rate of diastolic depolarization significantly correlated with contraction frequency in LMCs. Membrane potential recordings showed that diastolic depolarization preceded action potentials in all recorded cells, and both AP frequency and diastolic depolarization rate increased with pressure. Linear regression demonstrated a tight association (r²=0.8741, p<0.0001) between diastolic depolarization rate and AP frequency, while other AP parameters showed no significant pressure dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C85-C89 provide electrophysiological evidence with strong statistical support (r²=0.8741, p<0.0001) for the correlation between diastolic depolarization rate and contraction frequency. The biocytin-AF488 labeling confirmed recordings were from LMCs (C85). The lack of pressure effects on other AP parameters (C88) strengthens the specificity of the diastolic depolarization mechanism.

results.result: LMCs, or a subset of LMCs, are responsible for mouse cLV pacemaking. The combined findings from Ca2+ imaging, optogenetics, and electrophysiology support that LMCs are intrinsic pacemakers and that mouse cLVs do not require an ICC-like cell network to drive propagated contractions.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C122, C123 represent the main conclusion synthesized from multiple experimental approaches. The convergence of evidence from Ca2+ imaging (showing pressure-dependent diastolic transients only in LMCs), optogenetics (showing only LMCs can trigger contractions), and electrophysiology (showing diastolic depolarization correlates with frequency) provides strong support for this conclusion.

results.result: Deletion of Cacna1c, Gjc1, or Ano1 through PdgfrαCreERTM-mediated recombination did not significantly affect pacemaking in mouse popliteal cLVs. No significant differences in contraction frequency, ejection fraction, or vessel tone were detected in PdgfrαCreERTM-Ano1fl/fl or PdgfrαCreERTM-Gjc1fl/fl mice. PdgfrαCreERTM-Cacna1cfl/fl mice showed only mild increases in ejection fraction at 0.5 cmH2O and vessel tone.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 provide functional evidence from contractile tests in knockout mice. The lack of significant phenotypes in PdgfrαCreERTM-mediated knockouts, contrasting with previous Myh11CreERT2-mediated knockouts (C61), supports that PDGFRα+ cells are not involved in pacemaking. Statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA) and appropriate controls strengthen these negative results. The mild effects in Cacna1c knockouts (C65, C66) do not affect the primary pacemaking function.

results.result: Methylene blue staining revealed heterogeneous cell populations in isolated mouse IALVs, including cells resembling macrophages, mast cells, and a minor population with long thin axon-like extensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 describe direct observations from methylene blue staining experiments shown in Figure 1. The morphological descriptions are consistent with the imaging data, though the identification of cell types is based on morphology rather than definitive markers. This represents descriptive characterization rather than functional analysis.

results.result: Immunofluorescence staining revealed distinct cell populations in mouse IALVs. CKIT stained large ovoid mast cells, CD34 stained a contiguous population of fibroblast-like cells, and VIMENTIN labeled both LECs and CD34+ cells. Nearly all CD34+ cells were PDGFRα+, and these cells did not co-label with LMC markers (ACTA2, CALPONIN). PDGFRβ stained many CD34+PDGFRα+ cells and some LMCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C35 describe immunofluorescence observations from Figures 2-3. The staining patterns are well-documented with multiple markers and appropriate controls. The high colocalization between CD34 and PDGFRα (C32) is quantitatively supported by Pearson's coefficient (0.83) and Mander's coefficients (C37, C38). The spatial organization is confirmed by z-stack analysis (C40, C41).

results.result: Colocalization analysis showed high overlap between PDGFRα and CD34 (Pearson's coefficient 0.83, Mander's coefficients 0.80 and 0.87), while colocalization between MYH11 and PDGFRα was significantly lower (Pearson's coefficient 0.30).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 provide quantitative colocalization data from Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The statistical analysis using established colocalization metrics (Pearson's and Mander's coefficients) is appropriate. The high colocalization between CD34 and PDGFRα supports their use as markers for the same cell population, while the low colocalization with MYH11 confirms these are distinct from LMCs.

results.result: Inducible Cre-Rosa26mTmG reporter mice showed distinct recombination patterns. PdgfrαCreERTM drove recombination specifically in fibroblast-shaped cells but not LMCs or LECs. Myh11CreERT2 drove recombination in nearly all circumferentially oriented LMCs. CkitCreERT2 drove recombination only in sparse large ovoid cells on the vessel surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 describe confocal imaging observations from Figure 4. The distinct recombination patterns validate the specificity of the inducible Cre lines for targeting different cell populations. The tamoxifen-inducible PdgfrαCreERTM specificity (C43) contrasts with the constitutive PdgfrαCre (C42), demonstrating temporal control. These observations are critical for interpreting subsequent functional experiments.

results.result: RT-PCR analysis of FACS-purified cells confirmed the molecular identity of recombined populations. PdgfrβCreERT2-sorted cells expressed Pdgfrb, Myh11, and Pdgfra. PdgfrαCreERTM-sorted cells expressed Pdgfra and Pdgfrb but not Myh11. Myh11CreERT2-sorted cells expressed Myh11 and Pdgfrb but not Pdgfra.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 provide molecular validation of the Cre-mediated recombination patterns from Figure 4. The RT-PCR data confirm the expected gene expression profiles for each sorted population, supporting the specificity of the Cre lines. The absence of Myh11 in PdgfrαCreERTM-sorted cells (C48) is particularly important for ruling out LMC contamination in subsequent experiments.

results.result: scRNAseq analysis revealed three main cell clusters in mouse IALVs: LECs (Prox1+, Flt4+), LMCs (Myh11+, Cnn1+), and AdvCs (Pdgfra+, Lumican+). Very few Kit-expressing cells were observed. Pdgfrb was expressed in both LMC and AdvC clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 describe scRNAseq results from Figure 5. The UMAP clustering and marker gene expression patterns are consistent with expected cell identities. The low Kit expression (C54) aligns with imaging data showing sparse CKIT+ cells. The Pdgfrb expression in both LMCs and AdvCs (C55) explains the PdgfrβCreERT2 recombination pattern observed in C44. Appropriate quality control and filtering were applied (7435 of 10188 cells passed).

results.result: scRNAseq analysis showed that genes previously suggested to identify LMCs (Dpt, Pi16, Ackr3) were largely absent in LMCs and instead expressed in a minor AdvC population. Over 75% of AdvCs expressed Pdgfra, 65% co-expressed both Pdgfra and Cd34, and 72% of AdvCs expressing either marker co-expressed both genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 provide important corrections to previous literature and quantitative characterization of AdvCs. The finding that Dpt, Pi16, and Ackr3 are not LMC markers (C56) contrasts with Kenney et al., 2022, highlighting the importance of careful cell type identification. The high co-expression of Pdgfra and Cd34 (C58, C59) validates the immunofluorescence colocalization data (C37, C38).

results.result: PdgfrαCreERTM-sorted cells expressed transcripts for Cacna1c, Ano1, and Gjc1, genes critical for lymphatic contractions, pressure-dependent chronotropy, and electrical conduction.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 describes RT-PCR results showing expression of pacemaking-related genes in PDGFRα+ cells. While the expression is confirmed, the functional significance is tested in subsequent experiments (C61-C66) which show no pacemaking defects upon deletion. This highlights the principle that mRNA expression does not guarantee functional involvement (C134).

results.result: PdgfrαCreERTM-recombined cells expressed multipotency markers including Klf4, Ly6a, Gli1, Itgb1, Eng, and Cd44. CD34+PDGFRα+ cells co-stained with LY6A+, suggesting they may be primed to act as resident multipotent cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C68, C104, C105 characterize PDGFRα+ cells as potentially multipotent based on marker expression. The RT-PCR data (C67, C68) and immunofluorescence (C104) are consistent. However, functional multipotency was not tested, so this remains a hypothesis based on marker expression. The citations support the interpretation of these markers as associated with stemness (C104, C105).

results.result: Ca2+ imaging of CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f and PdgfrαCreERTM-GCaMP6f cells showed minimal spontaneous Ca2+ activity. Only 1 of 39 CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f cells and 3 of 21 PdgfrαCreERTM-GCaMP6f cells exhibited Ca2+ transients. CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f cells responded to compound 48-80 with prolonged Ca2+ events that did not alter LMC Ca2+ activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 provide negative results from Ca2+ imaging experiments in Figures 9-10. The low frequency of Ca2+ transients in these cell types contrasts sharply with LMCs (C79-C81), supporting that they are not pacemaker cells. The compound 48-80 response (C76, C77) confirms the cells are viable and responsive, and identifies them as mast cells, but shows they don't influence LMC activity.

results.result: Previous studies showed that genetic deletion of Ano1 or IP3R1 in LMCs using Myh11CreERT2 dramatically reduced contraction frequency and abolished pressure-dependent chronotropy, with diastolic Ca2+ transients absent in IP3R1 knockouts.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C110, C111 cite previous work by the authors supporting the IP3R1-ANO1 axis in LMC pacemaking. These citations provide context for the current findings and support the proposed mechanism. The consistency between the cited work and current observations strengthens the overall conclusion. However, these are not new findings from the current study.

results.result: Previous studies showed that targeted deletion of Gjc1 or Cacna1c in lymphatic muscle using Myh11CreERT2 resulted in contractile defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C92 are inferred from citations to previous studies showing contractile defects with Myh11CreERT2-mediated deletion of these genes. These provide important context for interpreting the lack of phenotype with PdgfrαCreERTM-mediated deletion (C61-C66). The contrast demonstrates that functional expression of these genes in LMCs, not AdvCs, is critical for pacemaking.

results.result: While a subpopulation of CD34+PDGFRα+ cells may share expression of critical pacemaker genes identified in LMCs, they do not appear to be involved in cLV pacemaking or contractile function under physiological states.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 synthesizes findings from gene expression (C60) and functional studies (C61-C66, C69-C74, C75-C78). The conclusion is well-supported by the convergence of negative results from multiple experimental approaches: no contractile defects in knockouts, failure to trigger contractions with optogenetics, and lack of Ca2+ transients during pacemaking.

results.result: Local photo-stimulation of PDGFRα cells failed to initiate contractions, while stimulation of Myh11CreERT2-recombined cells resulted in contractions indistinguishable from spontaneous contractions. Local optogenetic-initiated depolarization of single or few LMCs was sufficient to drive coordinated contractions, demonstrating the regenerative nature of the lymphatic muscle action potential and conducted activity at the tissue level.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 synthesize optogenetic findings and their implications. The contrast between PDGFRα cell and LMC stimulation (C119) is supported by quantitative data (C72-C74). The ability of single LMC stimulation to trigger vessel-wide contractions (C121) demonstrates both the regenerative AP and gap junction coupling, supporting the LMC pacemaker model.

results.result: The findings underscore the significance of lymphatic muscle Ca2+ handling as the driver of lymphatic pacemaking, which can be compromised in disease states leading to impaired lymphatic contractile activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C124, C125 provide broader context for the findings. C124 is well-supported by the current study's data on Ca2+ transients and their pressure-dependence. C125 cites previous work on disease states, appropriately extending the implications of the findings. This represents a reasonable extrapolation from the current results to clinical relevance.

results.result: The study assumes conserved pacemaking pathways across species, noting that mouse lymphatic vessels have similar pressure-dependent chronotropy and conduction velocity to rats and humans despite having a single LMC layer versus multiple layers in larger species. It is possible that vessels with multiple LMC layers need a network of ICLC to coordinate activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 acknowledge limitations and assumptions. C126 is stated as an assumption, C127 cites supporting data, C128 notes anatomical differences, and C129 speculates on possible species differences. These represent appropriate scientific caution about generalizing from mouse to human. The speculation in C129 is reasonable but untested.

results.result: The study acknowledges several methodological limitations including potential bias in scRNAseq from FACS purification, possible loss of large complex cells, stress-induced gene expression, insufficient cell marker staining for definitive identification, discordance between mRNA and protein expression, and variable specificity/efficiency of inducible Cre models with nonspecific recombination observed for GCaMP6f and ChR2.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C138 represent thoughtful acknowledgment of methodological limitations. These are appropriately discussed and do not undermine the main conclusions. The recognition that mRNA expression doesn't guarantee protein function (C134) is illustrated by the PDGFRα+ cell data. The Cre recombinase limitations (C135-C137) are acknowledged with appropriate controls used. This transparent discussion of limitations strengthens the overall credibility of the work.

results.result: The study demonstrates that lymphatic muscle cells (LMCs) are the pacemaker cells in mouse collecting lymphatic vessels. LMCs consistently displayed spontaneous, pressure-dependent Ca2+ events during diastole, optogenetic stimulation of LMCs induced propagated contractions, and the rate of diastolic depolarization in LMCs significantly correlated with contraction frequency.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirmed this central finding. Reviewer 1 stated the authors 'convincingly determine that lymphatic muscle cells are the origin of the action potential that triggers lymphatic contraction.' Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'convincingly demonstrate that only activation of lymphatic muscle cells produces coordinated lymphatic contraction and that only lymphatic muscle cells display pressure-dependent Ca2+ transients.' The editor described this as a 'fundamental discovery' using 'exemplary' approaches.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation experiments showed that only LMCs (Myh11CreERT2-ChR2) could initiate coordinated contractions (88.5% success rate), while stimulation of CkitCreERT2 or PdgfrαCreERTM cells failed to initiate contractions (3.25% and 3.03% success rates, respectively).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the optogenetic approach. Reviewer 2 highlighted 'the use of targeted expression of channel rhodopsin and GCaMP to test the hypothesis' as a strength. Reviewer 1 noted the experiments were 'rigorously performed' and 'the data justify the conclusions.' No concerns were raised about these optogenetic findings.

results.result: Ca2+ imaging with GCaMP6f revealed that only LMCs exhibited consistent spontaneous Ca2+ transients during the contraction cycle. Of 39 CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f cells, only 1 showed a Ca2+ transient; of 21 PdgfrαCreERTM-GCaMP6f cells, only 3 showed transients; while all 43 LMCs showed global Ca2+ flashes and 20 of 43 showed diastolic transients.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the Ca2+ imaging data as convincing evidence. Reviewer 2 stated the authors 'convincingly demonstrate...that only lymphatic muscle cells display pressure-dependent Ca2+ transients as would be expected of a pacemaker.' The editor noted 'the inclusion of scRNAseq and membrane potential data enhances a tremendous study,' indicating acceptance of the Ca2+ imaging results.

results.result: Membrane potential recordings in LMCs showed that diastolic depolarization preceded action potentials, and both AP frequency and diastolic depolarization rate increased with pressure. Linear regression demonstrated tight correlation between these parameters, while other AP characteristics remained unchanged with pressure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly requested and then accepted the membrane potential data. Reviewer 3 initially listed 'membrane potential measurements' as a weakness, but after revision stated 'I do not have any additional comments,' indicating the data addressed concerns. Reviewer 2 noted 'these weaknesses have been resolved by revision and addition of new and novel RNAseq data, additional colocalization data and membrane potential measurements.'

results.result: Pressure-dependent Ca2+ transient analysis showed that as intraluminal pressure increased from 0.5 to 5 cmH2O, the area activated by Ca2+ transients increased from 73.2±17.7 to 139.2±26.9 µm²/frame, and the number of transients increased from 2.9±0.4 to 5.2±0.6 per frame.
results.evaluation: Reviewers initially requested more quantitative analysis. Reviewer 2 noted 'the only significant weakness was the lack of quantitative analysis of most of the imaging data' but after revision stated 'these weaknesses have been resolved.' Reviewer 3 requested 'more quantitative measurements' but later stated 'I do not have any additional comments,' indicating acceptance of the added quantitative data.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed three main cell clusters in lymphatic vessels: LECs (marked by Prox1 and Flt4), LMCs (marked by Myh11 and Cnn1), and adventitial cells (AdvCs, marked by Pdgfra and Lumican). Very few Kit-expressing cells were observed, and Pdgfrb was expressed in both LMC and AdvC clusters.
results.evaluation: The scRNAseq data was explicitly praised by reviewers. The editor stated 'the inclusion of scRNAseq and membrane potential data enhances a tremendous study.' Reviewer 2 noted the weaknesses 'have been resolved by revision and addition of new and novel RNAseq data.' No concerns were raised about the scRNAseq findings in the final reviews.

results.result: Genetic deletion of Cacna1c, Gjc1, or Ano1 through PdgfrαCreERTM-mediated recombination did not significantly affect pacemaking in mouse popliteal collecting lymphatic vessels, in contrast to previous phenotypes achieved with Myh11CreERT2-mediated deletion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these negative results as supporting the conclusion that LMCs, not Pdgfrα+ cells, are the pacemakers. Reviewer 1 stated 'the data justify the conclusions' and the experiments were 'rigorously performed.' The lack of phenotype in PdgfrαCreERTM knockouts contrasted with LMC knockouts strengthens the main conclusion, which reviewers affirmed.

results.result: Methylene blue staining and immunofluorescence revealed multiple cell types in mouse lymphatic vessels, including mast cells (large ovoid CKIT+ cells), CD34+ fibroblast-shaped cells with 'oak leaf' morphology, VIMENTIN+ LECs, and DESMIN+ LMCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers initially requested more quantitative analysis of imaging data. Reviewer 2 stated 'the only significant weakness was the lack of quantitative analysis of most of the imaging data shown in Figures 1-11' but after revision noted 'these weaknesses have been resolved.' The characterization of cell types was accepted as part of the comprehensive study.

results.result: Immunofluorescence and colocalization analysis showed that nearly all CD34+ cells were also PDGFRα+ (Pearson's coefficient 0.83, Mander's coefficients 0.80 and 0.87), while CD34+ cells did not co-label with LMC markers. Colocalization between MYH11 and PDGFRα was significantly lower (Pearson's coefficient 0.30).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically requested that 'the colocalization analysis should be extended to show cells not expected to demonstrate colocalization as a negative control' and after revision stated 'these weaknesses have been resolved by revision and addition of...additional colocalization data.' The quantitative colocalization data was accepted.

results.result: Cre-reporter mouse studies showed that tamoxifen-inducible PdgfrαCreERTM drove recombination specifically in fibroblast-shaped cells but not LMCs or LECs, while Myh11CreERT2 drove recombination in nearly all circumferentially-oriented LMCs. CkitCreERT2 labeled only sparse large ovoid cells (mast cells).
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the genetic targeting approach. Reviewer 1 noted the study used 'genetic models to delete individual genes or detect cytosolic calcium in specific cell types' and the 'experiments are rigorously performed.' The specificity of the Cre lines was critical to the main conclusions, which all reviewers supported.

results.result: RT-PCR analysis of FACS-purified cells confirmed cell-type specificity: PdgfrβCreERT2 cells expressed Pdgfrb, Myh11, and Pdgfra; PdgfrαCreERTM cells expressed Pdgfra and Pdgfrb but not Myh11; Myh11CreERT2 cells expressed Myh11 and Pdgfrb but not Pdgfra. PdgfrαCreERTM cells also expressed Cacna1c, Ano1, and Gjc1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the RT-PCR validation of cell populations. Reviewer 1 stated 'the experiments are rigorously performed, the data justify the conclusions.' The molecular characterization supported the functional studies, and no concerns were raised about these findings in final reviews.

results.result: CkitCreERT2-GCaMP6f cells (mast cells) exhibited robust Ca2+ responses to compound 48/80 stimulation, but these Ca2+ events did not acutely alter LMC Ca2+ activity, indicating mast cells do not directly regulate pacemaking.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this as evidence ruling out mast cells as pacemakers. Reviewer 1 noted the study 'convincingly determine that lymphatic muscle cells are the origin of the action potential,' implicitly accepting the negative findings for other cell types. No concerns were raised about the mast cell experiments.

results.result: PdgfrαCreERTM-recombined cells expressed markers associated with 'stemness' including Klf4, Ly6a, Gli1, Itgb1, Eng, and Cd44. CD34+PDGFRα+ cells co-stained with LY6A+, suggesting they may be primed to act as resident multipotent cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the characterization of Pdgfrα+ cells as distinct from pacemaker cells. Reviewer 1 stated 'the data justify the conclusions and the limitations of the study are appropriately discussed.' The authors' interpretation that these cells are not pacemakers but may have other functions was accepted.

results.result: The study concludes that while CD34+PDGFRα+ cells may share expression of some pacemaker genes, they do not appear involved in pacemaking under physiological conditions. Instead, LMCs are intrinsic pacemakers, and mouse collecting lymphatic vessels do not require an ICC-like cell network to drive contractions.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly supported this main conclusion. Reviewer 1 stated the authors 'convincingly determine that lymphatic muscle cells are the origin of the action potential.' Reviewer 2 noted the study 'convincingly demonstrate that only activation of lymphatic muscle cells produces coordinated lymphatic contraction.' The editor called this a 'fundamental discovery' that 'establishes a new standard for the field.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge the assumption of conserved pacemaking mechanisms across species and note that while mouse vessels have a single LMC layer, larger species may have multiple layers. They suggest vessels with multiple LMC layers might need ICLC networks for coordination.

comparisons.comparison: Both support the main conclusion that LMCs are pacemakers. OpenEval R1 focuses on Ca2+ imaging evidence (C3, C4, C79-C84) showing pressure-dependent diastolic transients in LMCs. Peer R1 affirms the broader conclusion (C3-C7) that LMCs are the origin of action potentials, calling it a 'fundamental discovery' with 'convincing' evidence from multiple approaches.

Both address Ca2+ transient data in LMCs. OpenEval R1 provides detailed evaluation of pressure-dependent diastolic Ca2+ transients (C79-C84) with quantitative support. Peer R3 affirms the Ca2+ imaging showing 'only lymphatic muscle cells display pressure-dependent Ca2+ transients as would be expected of a pacemaker' (C75, C78-C81).

Both address quantitative analysis of Ca2+ imaging. OpenEval R1 supports quantitative data on PTCL area and frequency (C83, C84). Peer R5 notes reviewers initially requested more quantitative analysis and after revision stated 'these weaknesses have been resolved,' accepting the added quantitative data (C82-C84).

Perfect alignment on optogenetic findings. Both evaluate claims C69-C74 showing only LMC stimulation triggers contractions (88.5% vs ~3% success rates). OpenEval finds strong experimental evidence with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers explicitly praised the optogenetic approach as 'rigorously performed' with data justifying conclusions.

Both support electrophysiological evidence. OpenEval R3 evaluates correlation between diastolic depolarization and contraction frequency (C85-C89, r²=0.8741). Peer R4 notes reviewers initially requested membrane potential data as a weakness, then after revision accepted it, stating 'these weaknesses have been resolved.'

Both support the main conclusion. OpenEval R4 synthesizes evidence from multiple approaches (C7, C122, C123) concluding LMCs are pacemakers. Peer R1 affirms this as the central finding, with all reviewers explicitly supporting that authors 'convincingly determine that lymphatic muscle cells are the origin of the action potential.'

Both support the synthesized main conclusion. OpenEval R4 evaluates convergence of evidence for LMCs as pacemakers (C7, C122, C123). Peer R14 affirms the main conclusion (C103, C122-C124) with all reviewers supporting this 'fundamental discovery' that 'establishes a new standard for the field.'

Perfect alignment on knockout mouse data. Both evaluate claims C61-C66 showing lack of pacemaking defects in Pdgfrα+ cell knockouts. OpenEval finds functional evidence supporting that PDGFR⍺+ cells are not pacemakers. Peer reviewers accepted these negative results as strengthening the conclusion that LMCs, not Pdgfrα+ cells, are pacemakers.

Both address morphological characterization. OpenEval R6 evaluates methylene blue staining observations (C22-C25) as descriptive characterization. Peer R8 notes reviewers initially requested more quantitative analysis of imaging data in Figures 1-11 (including C22-C31), then stated 'these weaknesses have been resolved' after revision.

Both address immunofluorescence characterization. OpenEval R7 evaluates staining patterns (C26-C35) with multiple markers and quantitative colocalization. Peer R8 notes reviewers requested more quantitative analysis of imaging data and after revision accepted the characterization of cell types as part of the comprehensive study.

Both address marker colocalization. OpenEval R7 includes high CD34-PDGFRα colocalization (C32-C35) with Pearson's coefficient 0.83. Peer R9 specifically notes Reviewer 2 requested extended colocalization analysis with negative controls (C32-C39), and after revision stated 'these weaknesses have been resolved.'

Perfect alignment on colocalization quantification. Both evaluate claims C37-C39 providing quantitative colocalization metrics. OpenEval finds appropriate statistical analysis using Pearson's and Mander's coefficients. Peer reviewers specifically requested and then accepted the additional colocalization data including negative controls.

Perfect alignment on Cre line specificity. Both evaluate claims C42-C46 showing distinct recombination patterns validating Cre line specificity. OpenEval finds these observations critical for interpreting functional experiments. Peer reviewers affirmed the genetic targeting approach as 'rigorously performed' and essential to main conclusions.

Both support molecular validation of cell populations. OpenEval R10 evaluates RT-PCR data (C47-C49) confirming gene expression profiles and Cre specificity. Peer R11 accepts RT-PCR validation (C47-C49, C60) as rigorous with data justifying conclusions, supporting the functional studies.

Perfect alignment on scRNAseq findings. Both evaluate claims C50-C55 describing UMAP clustering and marker expression. OpenEval finds results consistent with expected cell identities with appropriate quality control. Peer reviewers explicitly praised scRNAseq data as 'new and novel' that 'enhances a tremendous study.'

Both address gene expression in PDGFRα+ cells. OpenEval R13 evaluates RT-PCR showing pacemaking gene expression (C60) but notes functional studies show no pacemaking role. Peer R11 accepts molecular characterization (including C60) as supporting functional studies, with no concerns raised.

Perfect alignment on PDGFRα+ cell characterization. Both evaluate claims C67, C68, C104, C105 characterizing these cells as potentially multipotent based on marker expression. OpenEval notes functional multipotency was not tested. Peer reviewers accepted the characterization and interpretation that these cells are not pacemakers but may have other functions.

Both address Ca2+ imaging in non-LMC cell types. OpenEval R15 evaluates negative results (C75-C78) showing low Ca2+ transient frequency in other cell types. Peer R3 affirms Ca2+ imaging evidence (C75, C78-C81) showing only LMCs display pressure-dependent transients, implicitly accepting negative findings for other cells.

Both address mast cell experiments. OpenEval R15 evaluates compound 48-80 response (C76, C77) identifying mast cells but showing they don't influence LMC activity. Peer R12 accepts this as evidence ruling out mast cells as pacemakers, with no concerns raised about these experiments.

Both support the conclusion that PDGFRα+ cells are not pacemakers. OpenEval R18 synthesizes findings from gene expression and functional studies (C103). Peer R14 accepts this conclusion as part of the main finding that LMCs are pacemakers, with all reviewers supporting the overall conclusion.

Both address optogenetic implications. OpenEval R19 synthesizes optogenetic findings (C119-C121) showing only LMCs trigger contractions. Peer R2 explicitly praises the optogenetic approach (C69-C74) as convincing evidence, which supports the broader implications discussed in C119-C121.

Both address broader implications. OpenEval R20 evaluates claims C124-C125 providing context and clinical relevance. Peer R14 accepts the main conclusion (C122-C124) as a 'fundamental discovery,' implicitly supporting the broader implications for understanding lymphatic pacemaking.

Perfect alignment on study limitations. Both evaluate claims C126-C129 acknowledging limitations and assumptions about species differences and anatomical variations. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to untested speculation. Peer reviewers explicitly stated 'the limitations of the study are appropriately discussed,' viewing this as appropriate scientific caution.
